Bay goby females attain a maximum total length of 10 centimeters [Li = 10 centimeters], a modest size characteristic of the Gobiidae; this ultimate length is reached after several years of steady somatic growth, with most individuals approaching the asymptote by the end of their third year. Field surveys from the northeastern Pacific, where this species inhabits soft-bottom substrates from the intertidal zone to depths exceeding one hundred meters, indicate that the transition to reproductive maturity occurs at a considerably smaller body dimension: puberty is triggered once females reach a total length of 4.5 centimeters [Lp = 4.5 centimeters]. This size threshold appears to be tightly linked to the onset of vitellogenesis and ovarian recrudescence, marking a clear shift from the juvenile growth phase to the adult reproductive phase.

The mass at which females first become reproductively capable, known as the wet weight at puberty, has been estimated at 0.8 grams [Wwp = 0.8 grams], a relatively low body mass that underscores the ability of this species to begin reproducing early in life. In contrast, the ultimate wet weight for females, representing the maximum asymptotic mass that a fully grown individual can achieve, is substantially greater at 9.3 grams [Wwi = 9.3 grams]; this value was derived from length–weight regressions based on field-collected specimens and reflects the accumulation of somatic and gonadal tissues over the lifespan. The nearly twelve-fold increase from pubertal mass to asymptotic mass indicates a prolonged period of post-maturation growth, consistent with an indeterminate growth strategy common among teleosts.

Newly hatched yolk-sac larvae of the Bay goby emerge from demersal eggs at a remarkably small wet weight at birth of 0.00016 grams [Wwb = 0.00016 grams]; this minute size, equivalent to 0.16 milligrams, reflects the limited yolk reserves allocated to each embryo and necessitates a rapid transition to exogenous feeding. The incubation period leading to eclosion is strongly temperature-dependent, and at a water temperature of 9 °C [T = 9 °C], the age at birth has been measured at 10.5 days [ab = 10.5 days]. This abbreviated embryonic duration at cool temperatures is typical of small-bodied gobiids that spawn in temperate coastal waters, where early hatching may reduce the risk of egg predation and facilitate the dispersal of the resulting planktonic larvae.

At a water temperature of 9 °C [T = 9 °C], the maximum lifespan of the Bay goby has been recorded at 7 years [am = 7 years], a longevity that is surprisingly extended for a fish of such diminutive adult size and suggests a relatively slow pace of senescence under the cool, stable conditions of its benthic habitat. This life span stands in contrast to many other small gobiids from warmer waters, which rarely survive beyond two to three years. The combination of early maturity and prolonged reproductive window implies that individual females can participate in multiple breeding seasons, potentially contributing to population stability over decadal timescales.

Under thermal conditions typical of the summer spawning season in its range, specifically at 13 °C [T = 13 °C], the maximum reproductive output of the Bay goby has been characterized by a combination of moderate clutch size and high spawning frequency. Females produce approximately 2.2 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 2.2 eggs per spawning event], a modest per-clutch fecundity that is offset by an exceptionally rapid reproductive cycling; gravid individuals are capable of initiating a new spawning event every day [F_R_i = event every day] during periods of peak activity. This daily spawning mode, sustained over the several-month breeding season, allows a single female to achieve a cumulative annual fecundity that is among the highest recorded for any gobiid of comparable body size.
